questions.model_answer: (1) Peramivir — intravenous (neuraminidase inhibitor; 300 or 600 mg, single dose or daily). (2) Zanamivir — inhaled (neuraminidase inhibitor, 10 mg twice daily); note inhaled zanamivir is impractical in severe disease, and intravenous zanamivir has been used/preferred in hospitalized or oseltamivir-resistant (H275Y) cases.

cohort_answer.text: Peramivir - 600mg IV daily x5 days, neuraminidase inhibitor. Zanamivir - two inhalations (10mg) BID for 5 days, neuraminidase inhibitor; not recommended for severe disease (requiring hospitalization) due to lack of data.

questions.question: Antivirals effective against influenza A virus.

parts.text: List three antivirals effective against influenza A.
Give the mechanism of action of each.

parts_raw.text: a) 3 antivirals available in Canada effective against Influenza A

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Oseltamivir (oral neuraminidase inhibitor). (2) Zanamivir (inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor). (3) Peramivir (IV neuraminidase inhibitor). [Amantadine/rimantadine are M2 inhibitors active only against influenza A but are now not recommended because of near-universal resistance in circulating H3N2 and A(H1N1)pdm09.]
b) (1) Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir): competitively and reversibly inhibit viral neuraminidase, blocking cleavage of terminal sialic acid residues so newly formed virions remain adherent/aggregated at the cell surface, limiting virus release and spread within the respiratory tract. (2) M2 (adamantane) inhibitors (amantadine, rimantadine): block the M2 ion-channel/proton flux of influenza A, preventing acid-mediated viral uncoating (dissociation of matrix protein from ribonucleoprotein) early in replication and hemagglutinin maturation late in infection; active against influenza A only.
questions.beyond_mandell: Which specific agents are marketed/available in Canada (e.g. peramivir, baloxavir availability) is a Canadian formulary/product-monograph point, not stated in this Mandell chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Flu A+B: Oseltamivir, Peramivir (licensed 2017), Zanamivir (inhaled). Flu A only: Amantadine (higher resistance rates recently). Not available in Canada: Laninamivir octanoate, Baloxavir (Flu A+B), Rimantadine (Flu A only). b) M2 inhibitors (Amantadine, Rimantadine): target M2 protein, inhibit viral uncoating/nucleic acid release/replication, active only vs Influenza A, widespread resistance now (not recommended empirically). Neuraminidase inhibitors (Oseltamivir, Peramivir, Zanamivir): competitively inhibit neuraminidase, stop virus release from infected cells and prevent new cell infection; resistance to Peramivir H275Y, Oseltamivir ~1% resistance H1N1, Zanamivir rare resistance.

Compare and contrast amantadine, oseltamivir, and zanamivir with respect to mechanism, the stage of the viral life cycle affected, side effects, and whether they are sensitive or resistant to seasonal (non-pandemic) H1N1, swine-origin H1N1, H5N1, and H3N2.

questions.model_answer:
a) High-risk adults (treat as early as possible): (1) age ≥65 yr; (2) chronic pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, hematologic, metabolic (e.g. diabetes) or neurologic disease; (3) immunocompromise, morbid obesity, pregnancy/≤2 wk postpartum, long-term-care residents, and all hospitalized patients.
b) High-risk children: (1) age <5 yr (especially <2 yr); (2) chronic medical conditions, immunocompromise, or neurologic/neurodevelopmental disorders; (3) long-term aspirin therapy (Reye syndrome risk).
c) Amantadine — M2 ion-channel inhibitor; blocks early viral uncoating (and late HA maturation); CNS/GI side effects (nervousness, confusion, insomnia); RESISTANT to seasonal H1N1 (since 2008-09), A(H1N1)pdm09 "swine", H5N1, and H3N2 (>95% resistant) — essentially no useful activity against current strains. Oseltamivir — oral neuraminidase inhibitor; blocks virion release/spread (late); nausea/vomiting; SENSITIVE to swine A(H1N1)pdm09, H5N1, and H3N2, but seasonal H1N1 was widely RESISTANT (H275Y, 2007-08). Zanamivir — inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor; blocks virion release/spread (late); bronchospasm/respiratory side effects; SENSITIVE to seasonal H1N1, swine A(H1N1)pdm09, H5N1, and H3N2 (retains activity against oseltamivir H275Y-resistant strains).
questions.beyond_mandell: The treatment indications / adult and pediatric risk-factor lists are from IDSA seasonal influenza guidance, not this Mandell chapter; the chapter supports only the mechanism, life-cycle, toxicity, and sensitivity/resistance comparison.

cohort_answer.text:
A - IDSA indications for treatment: Clinicians should start antiviral treatment as soon as possible for adults and children with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who meet the following criteria: Persons of any age who are hospitalized with influenza, regardless of illness duration prior to hospitalization (A-II). Outpatients of any age with severe or progressive illness, regardless of illness duration (A-III). Outpatients who are at high risk of complications from influenza, including those with chronic medical conditions and immunocompromised patients (A-II). Children younger than 2 years and adults >=65 years (A-III). Pregnant women and those within 2 weeks postpartum (A-III). Clinicians can consider antiviral treatment for adults and children who are not at high risk of influenza complications, with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who are either: Outpatients with illness onset <=2 days before presentation (C-I). Symptomatic outpatients who are household contacts of persons who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III). Symptomatic healthcare providers who care for patients who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III)

Adult Risk Factors list: Age >65, Chronic lung disease, CV/Renal/Liver disease, Hematologic, Metabolic condition, Immunosuppression, Neurological deficit/dementia, Obesity, LTC resident, Indigenous, pregnant

Pediatric Risk Factors (Last year's answer): Age <4 (especially if <2), Chronic medical conditions, Immunosuppression, Cognitive dysfunction/seizure/NM disorder, Long term ASA use (risk of Reye syndrome), Resident of CCC

Drug comparison table (partial, sensitivity columns for amantadine/rimantadine/oseltamivir/zanamivir order unclear): Activity against H1N1 non-pandemic | Sensitive | sensitive | Resistant | Resistant. Activity against H1N1 swine | Sensitive | Sensitive | Sensitive | sensitive. Activity against H5N1 | | | | Susceptible. Activity against H3N2 | Resistant | Resistant | | Susceptible

questions.question: Three cases of influenza occur on a hospital hematology/oncology ward, two confirmed as influenza A.
questions.question_raw:
Q6 (2003 AM)
3 cases of influenza, 2 of which are confirmed as influenza A in a hospital heme/onc ward.

parts.text: State the advantages and disadvantages of each.

parts_raw.text: What are three methods of prophylaxis?
B. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Antiviral chemoprophylaxis of patients (neuraminidase inhibitor, e.g. oseltamivir once daily). (2) Antiviral chemoprophylaxis of exposed health-care workers/staff. (3) Vaccination (immunoprophylaxis) of patients and staff; plus standard outbreak infection-control measures.
b) Chemoprophylaxis of patients — advantages: immediate protective effect, prevents spread to high-risk hosts, effective for controlling/preventing nosocomial outbreaks and additive to vaccine; disadvantages: cost, drug side effects, not all eligible (GI/renal), must recognize the outbreak first, and can select antiviral resistance. Chemoprophylaxis of HCWs — advantages: immediate effect, limits staff-to-patient transmission and sick days; disadvantages: cost, side effects, adherence, risk of selecting resistance. Vaccination (immunoprophylaxis) — advantages: durable, can be given pre-season, no ongoing drug administration, fewer GI side effects, protection additive to antivirals; disadvantages: ~2-week delay to protection (inadequate for an active outbreak), reduced efficacy in immunocompromised hosts or with poor strain match, and contraindications in some patients.
questions.beyond_mandell: The structured advantages/disadvantages and the defined prophylaxis durations derive from IDSA/PHAC outbreak-control guidance; the chapter grounds only that chemoprophylaxis is effective for nosocomial influenza, is additive to vaccine, can select resistance, and that vaccine protection is delayed.

cohort_answer.text:
Part 1: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis - Preexposure: > 3mo and high risk group, give for the whole season. Post exposure e.g. PrEP and PEP, either to patients or to healthcare workers. In setting of outbreak on ward generally give for at least 2 weeks and one week after onset of last illness. If exposed and able to be vaccinated, vaccine can be given followed by PEP for 2 weeks if good match. Immunoprophylaxis - generally given as PrEP. (NOTES: PEP: Within 48 hrs and for 7 days only in outbreak settings and special situations.)

Part B: Chemoprophylaxis to patients - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients. Disadvantages: Cost, patient side effects, not all patients eligible e.g. GI tract issues, Need to recognize outbreak before implementation. Can promote resistance.
Chemoprophylaxis to HCW - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients as often mediated by healthcare workers moving from room to room; can limit sick days and presenteeism. Disadvantages: Cost, side effects, need to recognize outbreak before implementation, can promote resistance.
Immunoprophylaxis of patients and healthcare workers: Advantages: Can be implemented in advance to prevent outbreak; can cover non-outbreak strains; does not require on-going drug administration and less GI side effects. Disadvantages: Delayed effect of 2 weeks for full benefit, during which may contract illness, certain patients may have contraindications to vaccine, May be ineffective if weak immune system or poor match, Cost (cost effective for high risk patients but perhaps not for healthy adults), side effects
